title: We like a good day. We also like knowing where the bathroom is.
summary: About An AUsome Life, a long-running New England family account focused on autism-inclusive life, practical access and useful recommendations.
search: Meet usWe like a good day. We also like knowing where the bathroom is.An AUsome Life is about the life we actually live: New England outings, clothes worth wearing again, hotels that work as home base, food people will eat, useful things that earn their space, and profound autism as one real part of the family story.No tragedy framing. No inspirational confetti. No pretending logistics do not exist.New EnglandClassic styleFamily travelUseful thingsOlder-teen access Wells Beach · family camera roll.One scoop in Lexington.The Book Barn, Niantic.A good life is allowed to be practical.Sometimes the difference between a lovely afternoon and an early exit is not profound. It is parking, a warm pool, the right food, a quieter corner, or having the charger you thought was in the bag. We write those things down.Our family includes an older autistic teen with very high support needs. We use profound autism for that experience. It tells you something important about support. It does not tell you the whole person.That perspective changes what we notice: the warm pool, the easier closure, the quiet place to pause, the product that removes a step, the restaurant that makes an ordinary dinner possible. These are one family's field notes, not a universal rulebook.High support needs can be profound. So can taste, humor, annoyance, adolescence and joy.Our language standardProfoundly Awesome Classic, not costumeWe like prep and New England style. We do not need every room to look as though a lobster trap has been promoted to furniture.Useful, not cleverIf the organizer needs its own organizing system, we have probably created a second problem.Age-respectful alwaysHigh support needs do not erase adolescence, personal style or dignity.Tell me the thingIs the pool warm? Does the zipper cooperate? Is there a surprise subscription? Put that near the top.

title: Accessibility is a field note, not a checkbox.
summary: How An AUsome Life researches, labels and presents accessibility information: mobility, terrain, sensory conditions, vision and hearing access, restrooms, changing equipment, parking and practical unknowns.
search: Access · the practical details left in Accessibility is a field note, not a checkbox. “Accessible” can mean almost nothing until somebody tells you about the hill, the gravel, the elevator, the lighting, the quiet corner, the restroom and the walk from the car. This is the standard we use when researching calendar events, Favorite Places and practical guides. We look for current official information first, then use public visitor reports as a secondary reality check when they add useful lived detail. We label uncertainty instead of turning it into a promise. What we checkEight questions before “accessible.”Not every venue publishes every answer. An honest “not confirmed” is more useful than a confident guess. Wheelchair + adaptive strollerStep-free entrances, ramps, elevators, doorway routes, seating, transfer points, wheelchair or mobility-device rentals and whether the route actually works beyond the lobby. Terrain + distancePavement, packed gravel, loose gravel, grass, roots, slopes, long walks, mud, snow and places where a wheeled mobility device may need more help than a general accessibility label suggests. Sensory + communicationNoise, lighting, crowd density, smells, startling effects, quiet spaces, sensory kits, visual supports, AAC-friendly participation, flexible movement, re-entry and whether “sensory-friendly” changes the environment or only the schedule. Blind + low-vision accessBraille, large print, tactile or verbal description, audio description, contrast, wayfinding and lighting changes. We avoid assuming that a wheelchair-accessible route is also an accessible visual experience. Deaf + hard-of-hearing accessCaptions, ASL interpretation, assistive-listening systems, visual announcements, hearing loops/headsets and how far in advance an accommodation must be requested. Restrooms + practical careAccessible and family restrooms, changing tables, and an adult-size or height-adjustable changing table only when a venue specifically publishes that information. We never imply that a particular family uses a facility simply because we report that it exists. Parking + arrivalAccessible spaces, drop-off, distance to the entrance, the best door to use, city parking realities, whether a shuttle runs and what happens after dark. Weather + escape planOutdoor exposure, snow, ice, rain, heat, muddy paths, low light, indoor backup options, break spaces and how easy it is to shorten the visit or leave. Evidence labels How strong is the information? Organizer-confirmedA current event page, ticket page, venue policy or direct accessibility statement. This is our starting point. Venue access guideA current accessibility, visitor, trail, seating or building guide that adds detail beyond the event listing. Public visitor reportA review or public Q&A can reveal practical realities—steepness, crowd bottlenecks, muddy ground, stroller frustration—but it is anecdotal and dated. We label it as such and do not let it override newer official information. Not confirmedWe looked and did not find a reliable current answer. That is a prompt to contact the venue, not permission to guess. See the method in useThe calendar now carries the field notes.Each dated listing can include mobility, terrain, sensory conditions, vision/hearing supports, restrooms, changing-equipment status, parking, weather, a map and a five-step visual visit card.Open the accessible New England calendar ↗ Editorial rules What we will not do. We do not convert “ADA accessible” into a blanket promise about the whole experience. We do not assume a venue has an adult-size changing table, sensory room, ASL interpreter, elevator or smooth terrain unless we can confirm it. We do not present a visitor review as a verified current venue policy. We date access research because buildings, programs, construction, staffing and weather conditions change. We do not diagnose what a person “should” need. The information is there so each reader can decide what matters for their own visit. The website itself Access should apply here, too. We aim for readable type, strong contrast, keyboard-accessible navigation, useful headings, meaningful link text, alt text for informative images, layouts that work on smaller screens, and controls that do not rely on color alone. Visual planners are editable because one person’s helpful wording or picture can be another person’s clutter. Our tools use visible words alongside icons, large controls, familiar examples, keyboard access and clear optional sections. Preselected settings make it possible to finish without adjusting every detail. Color choices always have written names; color alone does not carry an instruction. Our creative standardBeautiful, useful, respectful.Our default look is preppy New England: Nantucket light, Vermont warmth, recognizable objects and natural materials. Communication pictures keep a clear subject and a familiar word. Decoration belongs around the task, where it can add pleasure without obscuring meaning.We create and publish lawful, family-friendly content. Sexual content, graphic violence, hate imagery, exploitation, harassment and deceptive images of real people have no place here. We respect privacy, consent, intellectual property and the dignity of the people we portray. AI-created illustrations are identified as such and are never presented as family photographs or evidence about a real venue.The picture-card studio currently offers a reviewed starter collection and private, in-tab photo selection. It has no public upload gallery and does not generate new images live. Personal photos are not sent to us or automatically inspected. Use only appropriate pictures you are permitted to use. Any future live image-generation service must include input and output moderation before it is made available. If a page is difficult to use—or a field note is wrong, stale or missing—please contact us with the page and the detail that needs attention.

The trees have already done quite a lot of the work.Harvard, Massachusetts Read the story ↓The practical details ↓ Doe Orchards, Harvard, Massachusetts · from our family camera roll.The placeDoe Orchards in Harvard, Massachusetts.The pleasurePicking, looking, and being outside together.The practical bitUneven ground, fallen fruit, and the route back to the car.Before setting offCheck the farm’s own picking update and opening arrangements.Our Doe Orchards photographs have rather a lot going on: branches full of apples, fruit scattered across the grass, family members partly hidden by the trees, and Ruby joining the scene. Nobody has arranged the orchard for a magazine. That is part of its appeal.This is the kind of New England afternoon I want to keep: something seasonal, something ordinary, and enough room for the people who actually came. There is no prize for adding three more stops before getting home.Let the orchard be the outing.Apple picking gives a day a useful shape. You arrive, find the part of the orchard open for picking, choose some fruit, and eventually return to the car. The amount of wandering can belong to the family rather than an ambitious itinerary.Looking counts. Choosing counts. Spending time beneath a tree counts. For someone using an iPad or another familiar communication system, keep it available while the choices are happening. A beautifully prepared choice board in the boot of the car is having a rather limited day out.The orchard floor is part of the plan, too.Ruby in our family orchard photographs. Check the farm’s current animal policy before bringing a dog.Dress for what is underfoot.Our photographs show grassy ground and plenty of dropped apples. They are a useful reminder to think about shoes and the route, not just the weather forecast. Ask the farm about the current surface and distance if those details will decide whether the outing works.Our photo of Ruby records that family visit; it is not a current dog-policy notice. Farm arrangements, picking areas and rules can change. The same applies to the apples: a variety visible in an old photograph is not a promise about this week’s harvest.Keep the photograph. Keep the ending simple.I like the pictures with people doing the thing they came to do. A family photograph does not need everybody lined up and looking at the camera to be worth keeping.For another orchard afternoon, I would keep the plan similarly modest: check what is open, bring the ordinary essentials, and know how to finish. A bag of apples is quite a respectable result. Watch where time actually goes. What gets searched for, repeated, carried twice or abandoned on the nearest horizontal surface? Write down three difficulties, then choose the one that happens most often. “The chargers disappear” is a useful problem to solve. “We need to be more organized” is a lifestyle rebrand, and nobody needs one before breakfast. Put a frequently used item closer to where it is needed.Try an existing basket, tray or hook before buying a storage system.Remove an unnecessary step from a routine before adding a device.Ask the people using the space what they can comfortably see, reach and manage. Give the change a few ordinary days. A tidy photograph is pleasant; finding the keys on a rainy morning is the test that matters. If the system only works when everyone is at their best, it does not work yet. Count the whole job, not the marketing copy.+ Meals: opening to washing up When comparing a meal kit, prepared meal or recipe, read through every step. Count chopping, extra ingredients, pans, serving and cleanup as well as the advertised cooking time. Check portions and the household's usual food requirements before ordering. Choose a meal that fits the day available. A busy evening may call for familiar components assembled in a few steps. When someone wants to join in, offer a manageable part of the meal using their usual support, such as choosing between two options or placing napkins. Participation can fit around the meal already planned. Organization: after everything is put away Ask who will keep the system going. A container that needs to be unstacked, opened and carefully repacked may be too much work for something used several times a day. Labels help only when they make sense to the people using them. Cleaning: after the machine stops Look at emptying, cleaning, replacement parts and storage. For an appliance, check the manufacturer's instructions and what maintenance it expects. Include floor preparation or moving furniture in your estimate of the work it saves. A robot vacuum that requires a pre-vacuum is a little cheeky. Give technology a clear job.+ A household display might make today's plan easier to see. It also needs somebody to update it. Decide where the main calendar lives and who changes it, then avoid copying the same information into several places unless that genuinely helps. For any connected product, check what works without a subscription, what happens if the internet is down, and whether the controls suit everyone who will use it. Review the account and privacy settings before putting personal family information on a shared screen. The first-year cost Add the purchase price, required accessories, ongoing charges and expected replacement supplies. For a simple example, a $120 device with a $10 monthly plan costs $240 in the first year before taxes or extras. Check when a trial renews and how cancellation works before starting it. Before purchasing, write one practical hope: “We will be able to check tomorrow's plan in one place,” or “This will remove one regular cleanup step.” Keep the return deadline in view and try the product during ordinary use. If it creates more reminders, more accounts, more charging cables or more maintenance than the problem it solves, it has failed its interview. The things that stay should earn their space through usefulness, comfort or everyday pleasure. Those are all perfectly good reasons. Planning suggestions to adapt to the person and the day. Use established private records; do not enter personal care information on this public page.Return to the interactive guideThe details left inThe useful part, in full.Open just what you need.Put today’s plan first.+A useful handover helps the next person act. Begin with today’s date, the agreed time together, what the person is expecting and anything that has changed. Keep the long history in its appropriate record. Make the plan with the person receiving support, using the communication they prefer and any assistance they need. Explain who is arriving, what is happening and how the visit will finish. Offer choices within the arrangements that are genuinely available. Before responsibility changes hands Confirm the incoming person has arrived and has agreed to take over.Review the important changes and invite questions.Check they can access the needed supplies, contacts and current instructions.Confirm what happens if plans change or the return is delayed. When support needs uninterrupted coverage, do not rely on an unanswered message as a completed handoff. Show how communication works today.+Have the person’s usual communication tools available and ready to use, including a familiar backup if they have one. Show the incoming supporter where they are kept and explain any practical help needed to use them. Do not replace a familiar system with a new worksheet simply because the worksheet is convenient. Share the useful basics: how the person makes a choice, asks for help, signals a pause and indicates that they want to finish. If a signal is uncertain, say so. “This sometimes means a break; check with them” is more useful than presenting a guess as a fixed fact. The NJC Communication Bill of Rights supports meaningful choices, direct communication and access to working communication systems. The practical goal here is that the person can still participate when their usual supporter is away. Keep current care instructions alongside the short note.+The handover is a summary of arrangements, not a substitute for the person’s current care, medical or emergency plans. Confirm that the incoming supporter is authorized, trained where necessary and able to provide the support being transferred. Give them access to the actual instructions and essential information they need, through the established private channel. Do not omit a critical safety detail merely to keep the summary to one page. Equally, do not improvise medication directions, eating or drinking instructions, lifting methods or emergency procedures in this template. If instructions conflict, are out of date or cannot be accessed, resolve the issue with the appropriate person before the affected activity or handoff. Follow the existing emergency arrangements for urgent situations. The short handover template.+Use these headings in the private record or on the paper system you already use. The blank version is deliberately general. Add only the information appropriate for this recipient and setting; keep completed copies secure. Date and timePrepared: ______ · Support begins: ______ · Expected finish: ______ Today’s agreed planFirst: ______ · Then: ______ · The shorter version: ______ The person’s choicesWhat they have chosen: ______ · What is still open: ______ CommunicationTools and location: ______ · Useful partner guidance: ______ · Backup: ______ Food, drink and ordinary suppliesWhat is ready: ______ · Where the relevant current instructions are kept: ______ A pause or finishHow to check: ______ · Available place or option: ______ Changes that matter todayConfirmed changes: ______ · Question to resolve before handoff: ______ Current care and emergency instructionsPrivate location and version/date: ______ · Access checked: ______ Contacts and changes of planAgreed contact route: ______ · Backup route: ______ · Return-delay plan: ______ Responsibility acceptedOutgoing supporter: ______ · Incoming supporter: ______ · Time confirmed: ______ A completed handover can contain private information. Do not put it on a public noticeboard, leave it in a shared vehicle or paste it into an open online tool. Use the person’s agreed permissions and the provider’s requirements for storage and sharing. What a useful note sounds like.+Illustrative example: “Today we agreed on the library and home. The shorter version is returning the books only. The communication bag is beside the coat and has been checked. Please confirm the current return time with me before I leave.” This example does not contain the safety instructions for a real person. Those still need to be accessible to the person providing support. Close the handover at the other end.+Before leaving, give a brief factual update: what took place, what changed, anything needing attention and who has agreed to the next step. Complete required records in the proper system. Confirm that the next supporter has accepted responsibility where continuous support is needed. Revise the standing information when something changes. Remove an outdated copy so it cannot be mistaken for the current plan.
